New YORK, June 10.

MANILA, Jan. 1.-The following dis
patch, dated Fridy afternoon Decem-
Der 80, at Iloilo, Island of Panay, has
just been received here by boat. tele-
graphic communication with Iloilo not
having been resumed:


The situation at noilo is grave. Fif-
teen hundred natives, fully armed. are
at Melo, a surburb of Iloilo. Seventeen
thousand more, it is reported, are
awaiting orders to embark at several
points on the island Of Negros, fifteen
hours sail from Iloilo.


All the women have withdrawn and
many families have taken refuge with
the Americans. The rebels, after con-
sultation, insisted upon inaction until
General Aguinaldo had been heard
from. General Miller when this de-
mand was first made, declined to concede
them time and insisted upon an answer
being given him by noon to-day. At the
same time he gave assurances that
lives and property would be protected.


The foreign residents then petitioned
General Miller to grant the extension
desired by the rebels, as fight would
cause inevitable loss. This also Gen.
eral Miller refused.


AT the designated time native COM
mission again boarded the United
States transport Newport and asked
for delay, saying that they were unable
to control the army, which commanded
the city and surrounding country. Cen
eral Miller refused and prepared to land
forces, sending an emissary back to
Manila for instructions. 1t is said that
General Miller informed the ENJOYS
that the city must be turned over to
him, but he promised he would give the
insurgents twenty-four hours notice if
he later decided to lombard the place.


The insurgent newspaper in Iloilo
stated on Friday that the rebels were
fully determined to resist the Amer
leans. 1t was very evident the people
in the city expected bombardment.


The British second class cruiser Bon
aventura and the German cruiser Irene
were the only foreign warships at Ioilo.


The rebels are Strengthening their po-
sition and are preparing to resist. The
streets of Iloilo are full of armed SOL
diers who are constantly entering in
every direction. There is great excite
ment, which is increased by the appear
ance of the gunboat Ell Cano, flying the
Spanish flag. The public buildings,
churches and boats along the river are
filled with rebels.


The Newport's boats, as the dispatch
boat which carried this message is
about leaving, are being lowered with
four machine guns mounted in their
bows. The lighters are alongside the
United States transport Arizona. The
United States transport Pennsylvania
lies three miles to the south, with steam
up.

morrow with instructions to General
Miller from General Otis

Some towns and farming communities in
the Passaic River Valley, New Jersey, were
visited by tornado on last Sunday Con-
siderable damage was done to buildings
and felt mill at Browertown was wrecked.
Many imagine that tornadoes are confined
almost wholly to our large prairie States.
but the Eastern States really have their
proportion Of them. The tornado statis-
tics which the Weather Bureau has
gathered for twenty years show that Kan
sas, Iowa and some other Western States
have each been the scene Of more tornadoes
than any Eastern State but some OF
tho so-called tornado States" are each
larger than the whole OF New England,
and, area for area, the East has had it's fair
share The last number OF the Monthly
Weather Review says that the chance of
injuries from tornadoes Is just as great In
the East as in the West


The large Western States have suffered
unjustly from the use popular writer's have
made OF tornado statistics. Many persons
have been deferred from settling in them
on account OF the alleged dangers. These
States have been injured more by this evil
reputation than by tornadoes. Our weather
authorities assure the country that no more
destruction Ia done by tornadoes than by
lightning, high Winds hailstorms, droughts
and floods.

NEW YORK, February 1.-THE Ham
burg-American line steamer Fuerst Bis
marck arrived today from Genoa, Naples
and Gibraltar, after the longest passage
the steamer ever had made across the At
lantic and one of the toughest in the ex-
perience of her officers. The voyage from
Gibraltar to New York was made in twelve
days and seven hours, at an average speed
of 1882 knots per hour. Terrific gales from
the northwest and west were encountered
in swift succession from February ] to Z,
enormous seas frequently sweeping over
the vessel, smashing rails, doors and other
woodwork. Several ventilators were swept
overheard. and two boats were carried from
their chocks.


On February 3 one of the sailors. Otto
Lohse, German, was washed overheard
and lost. The hurricane force of the wind
was 50 great that for five days this great
and fast steamer could at times bare!y hold
steerageway, and rolled violently and la
bored heavily until the decks We're flooded
and many of the passengers were violently
i'll. For five days there was little rest
and sleep ON board OF the vessel. On ap-
preaching the coast intensely cold weather
was met, and the spray froze as it fell,
covering the hull, boats, bridges and rig
ging far up the masts with a heavy coat
ing of ice. When the Fuerst Bismarck en-
tered the Narrows she appeared like
veritable iceberg. Clambernng over her
side, the outer gangways were seen to be
so laden with ice that they appeared like
tunnels through some ice cave, with enor-
nous icicles hanging from the decks above
and passageways filled with ice and slush
several inches deep


The bulwarks and rails were swelled to
enormous proportions, and forward the an
chors, w1ndlasS and davitS We're covered
to the depth of a foot, while the bridges
We're one solid mass. The crew We're busy
breaking away the ice from the decks and
gangways in order to land their passen-
gers.

Pennsylvania and the ID Oregon regiments
and two guns to drive the rebels from the
American right flank. between the railroad

mountains, burning the villages behind the

rebels dropped to the rear and fired at the
advancing American troops from the jun
gle, apparently with the idea that this

treat of the Fiipinos. But, finding these
tactics Intellectual, these rebels scrambled
after the main body.

has been materially strengthened, and it is
not likely the rebels will succeed in getting
to as close quarters in the future as they
did yesterday, even if they return from the
mountains.

ASTORIA, Or, Aug. 24.-Three of the
ten-inch disappearing guns mounted at
Fort Stevens were tested to-day. The
test was made under the supervision Of
Captain Clark of the Ordnance Depart
ment, who is visiting the Pacific Coast
on a special detail for technical exam
ination and official report as to the
completeness and efficiency of all the
new batteries located along the coast.
Everything connected with the mech
anism and ammunition for the guns
was carefully scrutinized and measured
before the firing took place.


Captain Clark expressed the highest
satisfaction with the guns. The day
was perfect and the test was success
full in every respect. The projectile
used was a solid conical shot weighing
nearly 500 pounds Two of the guns
were fired at range of five and half
miles over the open water. AT the
point of impact with the ocean a col
umn of water spouted into the air sew
eral hundred feet. Commander Pat
terson aimed the guns and controlled
the firing squad. The last shot fired
was aimed at fixed target. which was
the extreme detached end of some old
piling over the jetty. The range finder
showed the point to be something over
three and a half miles from the gun.
When the smoke cleared away 1T was
found that the bunch of piles had been
fairly struck, one of them being broken
and carried away.

SANTA ROSA, Sept Last night
shortly after o'clock the Sonoma
Lumber Company's logging train
dashed into six fiat cars standing on
the main track just outside the COM
pany's yards at Guerneville. and as a
result three men were badly injured,
the engine demolished and three fiat
cars knocked into kindling wood.


The train was in charge of Conductor
Tom Lane, and is used by the lumber
company to carry logs from the lum-
Der camp in the woods near Bohemia
to the mills a Guerneville. The start
back from Mission Canyon had been
delayed and the trains crew was anXi-
Gus to reach home. When near the end
of the journey the crash came without
a moments warning.


Conductor Lane and Engineer Mort
Deal were hurled to one side of the
track and Fireman Ed Teadman to the
other. When picked up all three were
unconscious, and Lane and Deal have
been in that condition ever since.


How fiat cars happened to be stand
ing on the track has not yet been sat
isfactorily explained. When the train
left the yard earlier in the afternoon
the track was clear. The only explana-
tion possible seems to be that the cars
had been left standing on siding un-
secured and by their own weight start
ed down the grade and ran to the point
where the accident occurred. When
the crash came the engine was turned
completely around and fell with it's
wheels in the air.


Conductor Tom Lane and Engineer
Mort Deal are very badly injured and
both may die. Teadmans injuries were
less severe, but he will be laid up for
a long time. Deal is injured internally
and also about the head and back
Lane has cut three inches deep down
his hip, his back is hurt and internal
complications have arisen. Teadman
sustained a broken shoulder and was
also badly bruised. Medical attendance
was at once secured and everything
possible done to relieve the sufferinss
of the men,

TACOMA, 'Wr., March 4.-Chinese advices
received here contain the startling news
that thousands of rebels in the central
Chinese provinces of Honan, Anhui,
kiangsu, Human and Hupeh have combined
their forces and are wrestling immense ter
ritory from the authority of the imperial
government. The four walled cities of
Hungychai, Paiyicha, Kuyang and Meng-
cheng, together with seventy-five walled
villages, were captured by the rebels. They
are preparing to besiege Shuckou and are
surrounding Kanchou.


Late in January a series of battles took
place about Kuyang, in which 4, 700 rebels
are known to have been slain. Hundreds
of Chinese troops were also killed. The
rebels were literally moved down by the
quick-firing guns and magazine rifles with
which several regiments of the imperial
troops were armed. Later the imperial
troops succeeded in recapturing Hungychai
and might have followed up their success
had not several regiments Of raw troops
become panic-stricken and run away.


Changlo, which was captured by the
rebels some time ago, was retaken by the
imperial troops after fierce fighting.

smashed and washed away, the bridge rail-

was swept overheard, ventilators were lost
and the rails in many places bent and
broken. The steamer was unable to make
headway against the gales, and after six.
teen days of pitching, rolling and violent
wrenching put into St. Michaels on Fehru-
ary'15 for repairs and coal.

ANTLERS, 1. T., February 2S.-The race
tons court for the life of Walla Tonka
the condemned Choctaw Indian, was won
by hairs breadth by the courier, who
made the wild ride from South McAlester
to Aiikchi. Walla Tonka was to have been
shot Monday morning for the murder of
his uncle and came to the execution
grounds, as he had promised to do, having
been at liberty pending final action by the
court.


Last week a reprieve for a rehearing of
the case was ordered by Judge Clayton and
the courier dispatched on the eighty mile
journey. Rain was falling in torrents and
there was every cause for fear that he
could not make Alikchi, as he had but one
broncho to carry him the distance.
1t was after midnight Sunday morning
when the rider reached the flooded Kia-
nuchi river. Here he stopped till daylight,
and then, with his hand on the pommel of
his saddle, swan the stream with his pony.
The pony almost eXha austed when Big
creek was reached, and a long detour was
necessary, which caused hours of delay.
Night came and more rain, and when the
Seven Devils Hill was reached the bron-
cho fell to the ground with the rider and
both slept, though but ten miles from Alik-
Chi.


Before dawn they were up again, and
finally the broncho bearing the courier
staggered to the execution grounds, where
the witnesses, executioners and stolid Wal
la Tonka We're awaiting the fatal moment.
The Indian heard his reprieve without COM
ment and will appear before Judge Clayton
forthwith.

TACOMA, April 23-The steam


ships Glenogle and City of Kings


ton came into collision with a


L tremendous crash at 4:30 o'clock


this morning off Browns Point.
The Kingston was struck just back
of her boilers and cut almost
squareIy in two. In ten minutes her
hull had sunk and her upper works had
divided into two parts and were drift
ing about. They were subsequently
towed ashore by the Glenogle and tugs.
Nobody was killed, though the escape
of the Kingston's passengers and crew
was nothing less than miraculous.


The Kingston was entering port from
Victoria and the Glenogle leaving for
Victoria, en- route to Hongkong.
Browns Point is at the north end of
Tacoma harbor, six miles from the
ocean docks. Both steamships were
endeavoring to pass as near the point
as possible. The officers on each were
surprised to see the other steamship so
near in shore. The two vessels whistled
at about the same time, each signaling
to pass.


The Kingston attempted to pass the
Glenogle on the port side, and then,
realizing the certainty of a collision if
the Kingston attempted to get across
the Glenogle's bows, her engines were
reversed.


It was too late to avert the disaster
and the two vessels came together
with a crash. The Glenogle cut the

The purser and night watchman went
through the Kingston's deck, awaken
ing the sleeping passengers and the
crew.


The firemen poured up out of the fire
room and the engineers escaped quick
ly from the engine-room to the decks,
crOwding and jostling against each
other in their excitement. Many of
the crew escaped in only their night
clothes, while those sleeping more
lightly or nearer the deck were able to
seize some clothing. Men and women
struggled with each other for places in
the rigging, realizing that the steamer
was sinking.


The officers of the Kingston got out
the lifeboats and the Glenogles crew
had one of its lifeboats into the water
before the big liner had been stopped.


The sound of the crash and the
shrieking of whistles of the two boats
aroused the crews on the ships in the
harbor. Captain Powles of the ship
James Kerr ordered out a boat and
men to the wreck with First Mate
Hole. The second mate was sent on a
bicycle for a tug, and the tug Victor
put off to the scene.


AS the Kingston's passengers We're
being taken off, one of the masts top
pied over and fell across the deck
house, where a number of persons had
congregated, and the frail structure
gave way beneath the weight. Several
of its inmates were slightly injured. A
cabin boy floated off on a piece of
wreckage and was picked up by the
boats.


Passengers on the Glenogle were
much alarmed and rushed scantily clad
to the deck, ready for plunge into the
sea- Many of them were unnerved, and
the ships stewards piled lively busi-
ness with spirits and wraps. The
shock to the Glenogle was severe and
awoke every one instantly, nearly
throwing them from their berths The
Chinese crew was excited, and, al

Mongolians chartered and squealed as

was almost perfect aboard, and had
the vessel been in danger every one
would have been cared for by the
boats, which were manned also.

admit that they deserted the ship, but

them proper clothing in which to make
the voyage around the Horn. The bills
they contracted were all with the cap
tain's sanction, and the ship was liable for
them. The boys were R. T. Hainstock,
NJ. Watkins and A j. Lewis. When the
Hyderabad reaches England there will be
an investigation and the apprentices will
tell their side of the story. The friends
of the boys in San Francisco say they
were not to blame, and the whole trouble
arose over Captain Scott's refusal to sup
ply them with oilskns for the voyage
around the Horn.

The revised schedule has lifted President
Brush of the Cincinnati club out of quite a
big hole and incidentally robbed the Messrs
Nagners of picking up quite a big roll of
money. The original schedule left April
16. Sunday, in Cincinnati vacant, as the
Pittsburg club, which opens with the Reds
Saturday April 10, will not play Sunday
games this season. Messrs. Brush and
Wagner Immediately made arrangements
to run special train from Philadelphia to
Cincinnati, carrying the Senators between
the two points from Saturday evening until
Monday morning, landing the club back in
the Quaker city in time for the Monday
afternoon game. Sunday games in Cincin-
natl are winners under the most ordinary
circumstances, but being the first Sunday in
the season the game between the Cincin-
natis and Senators could have been depend
ed upon to attract an immense crowd. The
new schedule, which freezes out the Louis
Vile from eleven games. throws the Chi
cagos into Cincinnati April 16 and does
away with the extra expense of a special
train. II will doubtless prove a good thing
for the Washington club. as it can be rest
ing with the Quakers, and the conditions
will be equal when the two teams face eacn

From the Manila American, October 16.


Early yesterday morning, before day
light, scouting party of marines, consist
ing of Lieut.. Wynne and five men, left the
outpost at Fort Rice and secured the coun-
try around the causeway for some consid-
cradle distance. with excellent results, hav-
ing succeeded in locating several nests of
rebels, who certainly seem determined on
coming back to their old position, and
which the marines are determined to hold
against ell insurrecto opposition. In the
mist and darkness they advanced right up
to within fifty yards of the enemy's
trenches, when suddenly and without warn
ing they were fired on from three sides;
the insurrectos fired in continuous volieys.
for considerable time. and soon the two
companies who are stationed at the fort
were up and ready for action, but their SER
vices were not required.


Having flushed" the enemy and accom-
plished the purpose for which they were
sent out, the party was withdrawn without
a shot being fired on our side.


Great praise is due Lieut.. Wynne for his
courage and GOODNESS, and also 10 the men
who were with him, under such a heavy
fire, and the cool manner in which he
Unanswered his small party, taking them
back safe to camp without receiving a
scratch They arrived at the fort before it
was yet day. Later in the morning, about
10 o'clock, another party went out, and
while locating the rebel position they saw
five horses and young colt, which they
soon captured. This party was fired on by
two mounted officers of the insurrecto
army, who wore an attractive uniform,
with scarlet pants and artistic gold-laced
tunics of light blue material


The officers at the fort, after a consuta-
ton, made up their minds to shell the
rebels from the trenches, and the big guns
at the fort opened the ball shortly after 3
pm, and continued firing Tor nearly two

Ter, and the three-inch gun under Lieut.
Wynne threw shells right Into the enemy's
trenches. This officer has shown marvel
Gus accuracy in his firing, and his previous
artillery practice gives him a great advan-
tage both in aim and range.

WARDNER, Idaho, June 3.-There
are 345 prisoners in the stockade at
this place. Several new buildings con-
nected with the prison are under con-
struction, one, being guardhouse with
twelve stalls for solitary confinement of
incorrigibles. All the new buildings
and improvements indicate perma-
nency.


The Impeachment case against Sher-
iff Young and County Commissioner
Boyle will commence before Judge
Stewart at Wallace next Monday. 1t
is expected the inquest will be con-
cluded by next Saturday. More than
$50 witnesses have been examined and
valuable evidence secured. State Audi
tor Sinclair left for Boise to-day and
will return Wednesday.


There is difficulty in securing miners
in Canyon Creek. The union men are
threatening new arrivals despite the
presence of United States troops.


BOISE, Idaho, June S.-The Boyle
habeas corpus case was continued be-
fore Judge Beatty to-day. The Judge
would not issue the writ, basing his ac-
ton on the defects of the petition. He
finally denied the alternative writ and
ordered the Attorney General to show
cause why habeas corpus should not
issue. This phase of the matter will be
argued on Monday.


WALLACE, Idaho, June S.-Two
Canyon Creek mines will be running
tomorrow. The Standard started to-
day with a small force, but will not at
tempt to take out ore until more men
are engaged, only development work
being done Workmen were sent from
here to Burke to-day to start the Hecla
mine tomorrow morning with a full
force This morning the train from
Burke was ditched, but in spite of that
nearly 300 union men and women
walked to this place to attend the
funeral of Michael Devine, who died in
the Wardner Prison on Thursday.

HONOLULU, May 13.-The army trans
port Warren had a narrow escape going
out of the harbor on the 1st inst, and it
is due to Captain Macauley's skill and
carefulness that she got out in safety.
Some malicious person aboard the trans
port fastened the clutch that connects
the hand and steam steering apparatus,
so that the rudder could not respond to
the wheel.


The Warren cast off her lines at $50
clock from the Oceanic wharf. Captain
Macauley was the ~ilOt He swung her
around by her stern and bow lines until
she was in perfect position to move out
of the harbor Then she started ahead.
When she got to the point near the light
house where the turn is made into the
channel the vessel failed to respond to
the wheel. Captain Macauley ordered the
engines reversed. and backed up. The yes
sci backed true and another start was
to the wheel. Captain Macauley was now
convinced that something was wrong with
the steering gear and backed into good
position. and sent lines to the Pacitic Mail
wharf to hold the vessel in position
while an examination was made. 1t was
then that the discovery was made that
the clutch had been disconnected. The
connection was made and guard placed
over the clutch to prevent any more tam,
pering with it, and then the vessel moved
out under perfect control.


While the steering gear was disconnect-
ed another untoward Incident occurred,
not important in itself, but significant in
connection with the other This was the
breaking of the telegraphic connection
between the bridge and the engine room.
The speaking tube connection was, how
ever. still intact.


The discovery of the trouble with the
steering gear in time found the vessel at
a point where it could be safely handled:
But had the discovery been delayed until
later. the most serious consequences
might have ensued. 1t is supposed the
motive of this tampering was to delay the
departure. of the vessel. The belief on
shipboard was that it was done not by
the soldiers. but by some of the ships
crew.

well-known breeder of pigeons has been

leased. 1t was noon the following day be-
fore the two that had pointed for home re-

only thing which brought them through
was the fact that the men were green
horns and failed to realize their danger.
Experienced seamen, he said would have
deserted the ship and taken to the boats
in mid-ocean.


The Manauense is a chartered ship flying
the British flag. She belongs to firm
which the officers say bought her for S45,-
600, and they claim efforts were made to
sell her to the government for s150,000.
She started from San Francisco accom-
panied Dy transport Hekln, Whlcn car


ried the rest of the 31st Regiment and en-
countered heavy seas to Honolulu. but
without accident. Soon after the start from
San Francisco it developed that she was
undermanned and soldiers had to be de-
| tailed as firemen, coal passers and walters,
and to do other work.


Before reaching Honolulu the crew con-
cluded that the ship was not safe, and the
majority agreed to desert
Though they were closely watched many
of the crew succeeded in getting away, and
the Manauense left Honolulu with less
than half her crew.


The captain of the transport, on Novem-
Der II, told Col. Hayes that the vessel had
sprung a leak, and investigation re-
suited in finding several feet. of water in
her hold.


The steam pumps were tried but failed to
work, and there were no hand pumps on
board. However, forty-six buckets were
found, others We're tmprcvised and the sol
dlerS not employed in working the ship
We're organized into five shifts. and, strip
ped and forming lines, they began bailing,
the officers working with the men, passing
the buckets, which were sent up to the
deck by a WindlaSS.


The longest time shift could stand was
two hours, and often the period was not
longer than half an hour.


The day the leaking discovered the
machinery collapsed and the electric-light-
ing plant and evaporating, distilling and
refrigerating apparatus became useless.
There were no lamps, ard the few candles
were exhausted after few days.
During the last week of the passage the
Manauense was in utter darkness at night.
She had been rolling in heavy seas all the
way, but on November - she encountered
a typhoon and pitched and tossed alarm
ingly. The Pekin became separated from
the Manauense in the storm. The water


rose rapidly, and the bailing force was
doubled.


Many of the buckets were smashed. and
barrels and boxes were substituted for


them, the men working in darkness, with
pieces of iron and planks shifting or being
violently washed among them. The fire
men could only feed the fires by being
lifted the shoulders of other men
through water waist deep.
The typhoon lasted two days and half,


and in the midst of it the engines stopped.
The officers then held a council and found
that there were 420 persons on board, with
l:feboat accommodation for 213.
In the meantime the men below, ignor-
ant of their extreme peril. were passing
buckets and singing What the He'll Do
We Care?' while the ship rolled helpless on
the ocean, with matches closed.
The heat was intense until the typhoon
passed, and then the Pekin. which had re-
traced her course about seventy miles,
came alongside the Manauense. which was
rolling SO heavily that the soldiers in the
hold could at each roll the Pekin
through the matches overhead.
Col. James S. Petit, commander Of the
31st Regiment, ordered the Manauense to
proceed to Guam and await relief. but the
captain of the Manauense demurred, the


officers say, because the government was
renting the ship for $500 day.
Throughout the remainder of the voyage
the engines of the Manauense failed fire.
quently.


The meat and vegetables rotted because
of the failure of the refrigerators and We're
thrown overheard.


After the storm the water supplied to the
ship at Honolulu had to be used for the
boilers, and there was little or none for
drinking. It is asserted that during the
last week of the voyage the men lived al
most entirely whisky, beer and hard
tack.


The officers and soldiers declare that the
engineers We're grossly Incompetent. The
officers also say that the behavior of the
troops was beyond praise For days they
worked in the dark, suffocating hold, with
later sometimes up to the shoulders and
piaHS- about, enGangering life and
limb.


The captain of the ship promised the men
twenty-five cents an hour for baiiing, but
he now proposes to pay them S130 a day.
The soldiers talk of attaching the ship.
The regiment will proceed to Zamboanga
on the Pekin to garrison several ports on
the Island of Mindanao.

NEW YORK, April 13-Detectivs Doyle
killed Martin Carey in Gustav Spohrs
saloon. Montrose avenue, Williamsburg, at
o'clock this morning. The bullet pierced
the victims heart.


He also shot and seriously wounded
August Miller the ball going through his
left hand. Another shot fired missed its
intended victim.


The detective, in citizens dress had been
in the saloon two hours, drinking with
young woman who gave her name as Mag
gle Miller When SpOhr announced his in.
tention to close the saloon Doyle refused to
leave with his companion. An alteration
ensued, and Spohr, his wife and two men
who wers in the place attempted to put
Doyle out. The latter and his companion
retreated to the rear door and started UP a
stairway. At the fourth step Doyle stop
ped, drew pistol and cried: Now come
on out here, all of you, and will kill YOU
ALL one at time" Carey advanced to-
ward him, and as he did so Doyle took de-
liberate aim at him and fired. Carey gave
one scream of agony, clasped his hand to
his left breast, and with thu cry. My God.
L have been killed." staggered from the
place. He ran about seventy-five feet and
dropped dead on the sidewalk.


The detective did not pause an instant.
but fired two more shots. One of them
went through August Millers hand The
other bullet crashed through the doorway.


Police officers who heard the shooting
came up and found Doyle hidden in Spohr.s
apartments. He came out when summoned
but meanwhile he had thrown away the
pistol, and denied having done any shoot
ing. The affray attracted a large crowd.
and the police had to hurry Doyle away to
save MIN from summary vengeance.

LONDON, Sept 1S-Olive Schreiner
(Mrs. Cronwright) contributes an elo-
ouent cable letter on the situation to
the Manchester Guardian. She says;


Let England clearly understand
what war in South Africa means. The
largest empire the world has ever seen
will hurl it's full force against a small
state and about 10000 men, including
lads of sixteen and old men of sixty,
without a standing army or organized
commissariat. The entire little people
will have to resolve itself into an army
of their wives and daughters, who will
prepare the bread and meat the farmers
will put in their saddle bags when they
go to meet the enemy. To-day the wo-
men Of the Transvaal are demanding
guns that they may take their part in
the last stand. We may crush the little
people with the aid of Australians and
Canadians, since the British Isles seem
unable to crush them alone. We may
take their land and lower the little flag
of his independence, so dear to the
Boer, but we shall have placed a stain
upon our own that centuries will not
wash out. Only the international spec
ulator who, through persistent misrep-
reservations and by means of the press,
has wrought this evil, will gain and fill
his already overloaded pockets with
South African gold"

IN England Christmas is celebrated with

Significance rarely put into execution, ac-
cording to the women; the music, riddles

ry-making, are all familiar to Christmas

mas celebrations have, however, largely lost

gland. and family reunions and evergreen
trimmings are nearly all that remain of the

steamship Laurada, which lies wreck in

Laurada, Capt. Frank White, left Seattle
September u, for Cape Nome, with crew
of forty-eight officers and men and twenty
passengers. She carried a full cargo of
general merchandise, hay, lumber, cattle
and sheep. The Laurada encountered
rough weather from the start, and on Sep
tember q she sprung leak. She was run
into the shallow waters of Zapadine bay,
where her crew, passengers and cargo were
landed and housed In several abandoned
cabns- The Corwin, attracted by signals,
took aboard the crew and passengers, TAX

remainder to Seattle.

Spanish war a flibuster and blockade

TACOMA, April 5.-The sailor question
is getting more entangled on the Sound
every day Five alleged cases of shang-
haing have been reported within forty
eight hours at Port Townsend First two
H-year-old Fremont boys were induced
to go to Port Townsend to work They
signed shipping articles there, not know
ing their import. Late at night they
were taken aboard the bark Kliclxitat
which sailed Immediately for Honolulu.
One of them jumped overheard and es-
capped, but his companion, named Saun-
ders, remained aboard. Saunders father
has applied for police assistance in nber-
ating his son.


Three men are alleged to have been
shanghaied aboard the British bark Kate
f. Troop, from Port Blakeey for Guaya-
quill. When taken aboard at Port Town
send they refused to sign articles and were
finally put ashore. They complained to
Federal Court Commissioner Swan, alfeg-
ing that Captain Fownes of the Troop
had paid bloodmoney for them. War
rants were issued for two sailor board
ing-house runners, but they had left
town before the Deputy Marshal could
arrive from Seattle to arrest them.


The difficulty at Port Townsend is due
Union, but more to the advantage pos
sessed by boarding-house men there. who
know ship has no chance to get beyond
them and are inclined to be arbitrary in
their terms. Several crews have been
shipped from Tacoma to Port Townsend
and the demand for non-union sailors Is
greater than the supply.

The cortege moves with solemn tread,
The crowded streets along;
And hushed, in presence of the dead,
Is all the gathered throng.

flushed, in the presence Of her dead.

text:
Written on the occasion of the reinterment in n
fucky of the troops from that state who fell in
Mexican war.J
The muffied drums sad roll has beat
The soldiers last tattoo!
NO more on life's parade shall meet
That brave and fallen few
On Fane's eternal camping ground
Their silent tents are spread;
And Glory guards, with solemn round
The birouac of the dead.
No rumor of the foes advance


Now swells upon the wind;
No troubled thought at midnight haunts
OF loved ones left behind;
No vision of the morrow's strife
The warriors dream alarms.
No braying horn screaming fife
AT dawn shall call to arms.
Their shivered swords are red with rust.
Their plumed heads are bowed
Their naughty banner. trailed in dust,
Is now their martial shroud:
And plenteOus funeral tears have washed
The red stains from each brow;
And the proud forms by battle gashed,
Are free from anguish now.
The neighing troop the flashing blade,
The bugie's stirring blast,
The charge, the dreadful cannOnade,
The din and shout, are passed;
Nor wars wild note nor glory's peal,
Shall thrill with fierce delight
Those breasts that never more shall feel
The rapture of the fight.
Like the fierce northern hurricane
That sweeps his great plateau,
Flushed with the triumph yet to gain,
Comes down the serried foe.
Who heard the thunder of the fray
Break DER the field beneath
Knew well the watchword of that day
Was victory or death.
Full many norther's breath has swept
Oer AngGstura's plain,
And long the pitying sky has wept
Above its mOldered slain;
The ravens scream eagles flight,
Or shepherds pensive lay,
Alone now wake each solemn height
That frowned Ger that dark fray.
Sons Of the Dark and Bloody Ground,
Ye must not slumber there,
Where stranger steps and tongues resound
Along the needless air;
Your own proud land heroic soil
Shall be your filter grave:
She claims from War its richest spoil,
The ashes of her brave.
Thus meath their parent turf they rest
Far from the cory fed,
Borne to a Spartan mother breast
On many bloody shield.
The sunshine of their native sky
Smiles sadly on them here,
And kindred eyes and hearts watch by
The heros sepulchre.
Rest on, embalmed and sainted dead!
Dear as the blood ye gave;
No impious footstep here shall tread
The herbagc of your grave.
Nor shall your glory be forgot


While Fame her record keeps,
Or Honor points the hallowed spot
Where Nalor proudly sleeps.
Yon marble minstrers voiceless stone
In dea thless song shall tell,
When many a vanished year hath flown,
The story how We fell:
Nor wreck, nor change, nor winters flight,
Nor Times remo-seless doom,
Can dim one ray OF holy light
That gilds sour glorious tomb.

After brief hearing yesterday after

brief the hearing elected facts of inter
est regarding the peculiar transactions

rights and her property.


Miss Sankey told the story on Wednes-

tangle of questions and answers the fact

bling, broken hand.

alyzed the young woman gave an eX-
PLANTATION of the matter in which her

In addition to the threatened expose, as

1--WE went shopping together" said the

In conclusion the witness, in order to

the night with her. The next morning
Mrs. Coggins called at the house where
the lady friend resided and said that if

knock it down. Miss Sankey opened the

osition signed by Charles S. Coggins was

sion brings out one important fact-Cog-
gins acknowledges that he never paid
tate. Miss Sankey alleges that he has

SANTA BARBARA, April 13.-Aided
by her gardener, Mrs. Broome. promi-
nent Santa Barbara lady. held fourteen
workmen and the City Marshal at bay
One year ago the City Council notified
Mrs Broome TO destroy a hedge that
obstructed a public highway, and which
extended sixteen feet beyond her prop
erty.


The matter of establishing the official
grade on that street has been agitated
for a long while, and finally the SEN
sation of the obstruction reached a
climax this morning. Marshal Martin,
accompanied by his deputy and force
Of workmen, went to the place 10 dis
charge their duties, but met with de-
termined resistance on the part of Mrs.
Broome and her hired man. She seized
a pick. made for the officer, and struck
him blow on the shin which may
prove serious. Martin took the imple-
ment from her and she Immediately
made straightway for another, but be-
fore she had taken few steps she was
overpowered and arrested.


They next proceeded to arrest the
hired. man. Alexander VaneZuela, who
was armed with q revolver and club
Had il not been for the extreme care
they used in performing the operation
if might have cost the life of one of the
men. Martin attracted Nanezuela's at
tention while Richardson, his deputy
came noiselessly from behind and dis
armed him.


Both Mrs. Broome and her man were
conducted to the City Jail. When
brought into the Police Court she was
read the complaint charging her with
resisting an officer and informed of the
nature of the offense. Although bail
was offered her, she refused, and stated
that she would not employ counsel
She further stated that she had been
unlawfully arrested and would main
tain that position, on account of her
nationality, being British, and will
bring the matter into the Federal court


In the meantime the work of remoY-
ing the obstructions over which the
trouble occurred went on and was soon
completed. The prisoners were released
on their own recognizance. This is a
high misdemeanor and must be tried in
the Superior Court.

ium. still 1t shows that the powers are

+ RADE conditions showed some change last

activity everywhere varied by the state
ment that the retail and distribuve trade had fallen
on in localities, accompanied by impaired collec-

352 per cent over 1898 and 57.3 per cent 1892

in iron and steel the heaviest known early

last year And when it is seen that prices keep up
all along the line there is believe that the
slight falling off in the movement OF merchandise here
and there due to anything else than the unreasonable
warm weather.


The great staples stand about the same as last week
While iron and steel are still at high pressure the
minor metals such as tin lead and "copper" are weak

ulative demand. The failures for the week were 100

Conditions this coast continue brilliant. All
classes of trade active and prosperous and those
large business for months. The export demand for
all sorts OF commodities, both foreign and Govern
ment account better than it is to-day, the
only drawback being a continued scarcity of cars.

for the latter, and heavy orders for the former on
Hawaiian account Provisions live stock hides WOOL
dried and canned fruits, wine oils, eather-in fact
almost everything that California produces-are more
active than for years. and what is still better, at
unusually high prices The early rains have greatly
enhanced the general confidence in the future and
credits accordingly easy, while there are no COM
plants of collections from any quarter Failures are
few and small rule for when business is as brisk
as at present it is easy matter to meet liabilities
The prediction made early in the year that 1900 would
be the banner year for California is being abundant1v

Four Omaha firemen were shocked to
death the other night while fighting a fire.
They were hoisting anextension ladder when
the apparatus came in contact with a naked
electric light wire. Instantly the deadly
current sprang down the metal fastenings
of the ladder, and the men at the crank fell
to the ground, two instantly killed. two
mediately afterward. Two other fremen
were seriously shocked. Here again the
miserable method of stringing these danger
Gus conductors through the air makes good
its threat against human life. The danger
is not only to the brave fellows who man
the steamers and trucks, but to the prop
erty owners and householders, whose build
ings may be destroyed because the fremen
are prevented from fighting the flames by
the wires, whose families may be DESTROYED
while the apparatus is being extricated
from the maze of electrified metal The
menace affects every citizen. Not until
every wire of every kind electric light
street car, telegraph and telephone Is put
under the ground and exposed only at the
point of immediate use is the city safe.
Washington hopes to attain this ideal soon.
1t has accomplished much already to that
end But there are yet many wires over
head. and these must all be buried Those
four victims in Omaha are sacrifices to the
sloth and penuriousness of the municipality
and the corporations

NEWPORT NEWS, Va, September O.
The battle ship kearsarge, just finished at

She cast off from the pier at the yard at q

teen minutes later Backing out into the
channel, the huge ship made a graceful
half turn and headed straight for the capes.

the large crowd of spectators cheered them
selves hoarse The kearsar2e, with main
armament and stores aboard, was loaded
almost to her draught. AS she passed there
was scarcely a ripple at her bow. Just off
the city more steam WAS put on. and the
ship percep:ibly increased her speed veer-
ing in toward shore she did She

1t was the intention of those in charge to

capes and put her through the evOlutions
necessary to show her capabilities. She is
expected to return to the yard about 8
o'clock tonight. Within the capes the
kearsarge acted like a perfect ship. an
swering to the guiding touch though IN
stinct with life. Her engines worked with

hitch. The behavior of the ship gives

w. A. Post of the company and other high

- LONDON, Oct. THE most important
news comes from the Transvaal tonight,
which, If true, probably indicates that the
South African republic is about to yield,
or in any case that the Beers have aban-
doned all ideas of invading Natal.


The news is comprised in a cablegram
from Newcastle. Natal, which says that
the farmers who arrived there to-day
from the Buffalo River state that the
Beers are returning to their homes, leav-
ing patrols along the river. The comman-
ders still remain on the Free State bor-
der.


The dispatch also says that the feeling
at Newcastle now is that the Beers do not
intend to attack that place and that the
evacuation Of the town was premature


A dispatch from Durham also states that
the excitement there has abated, owing to
the Beers holding back from the frontier


This retirement Of the Beers is what the
British war authorities have expected, as
their defective commiSsariat would pre-
vent them from long remaining massed
along the border kilograms received here
lately have made frequent reference to the
scarcity of forage and supplies in the Boer
laagers and have stated that many of
those in the camps were inclined to strike
for their homes unless active operations
were undertaken Immediately


The dispatch from Newcastle looks as
though they had done as they threatened
and had abandoned the idea Of fighting.
Meanwhile further transports from India.
with two field hospitals and hussars, have
arrived at Durham and the men and ma
terial were forwarded to Ladysmith in
stantly. General Sir George Stewart
White, V. c., who will command the Brit
ish forces in Natal, has also arrived and
landed. He was greeted by a large crowd.
General Sir William Symons, his second

him, showing that he does not fear a
Boer incursion into North Natal A num-
Der of other officers were present and the
whole party left by train for Pieter-
maritzburg amid great excitement and
cries of Remember Majuba"

A dispatch from Santiago de Cuba yester-
day says: Five men are dead and ten
wounded as a result of fight last night
between gendarmes and disappointed Gu
ban soldiers, at Cuevitas three miles from
Santiago. where the payment of the Cubans
troops Is progressing. Five thousand Gu
bans gathered there to receive pay. and af-
ter three days only $50 had been paid,
Thousands who had been disappointed at
other points had come to Cuevitas. as the
last place Of payment in the province.


The imperfect list caused great dissatfs-
faction. and rumor circulated Yesterday
that the paymasters would leave today
alarmed the men who had not been paid
They began to collect in groups and to show
their annoyance. Finally their threats be-
came serious.


Captain Baliat, with twenty gendarmes.
was present to preserve order among the
applicants, and the United States troops
protected Colonel Moale the officer having
charge OF the payments. Suddenly Captain
Baliat, who was mounted. was surrounded
by mob. struck by stones and bottles and
shot in the arm. His men promptly fired
volley into the mob, three persons being in.
stantly killed and thirteen wounded two
of whom died this morning.


Colonel Moale's guard promptly surround.
ed the money office, but took no part in the
fighting.


For few minutes there was a lively corr
fiict, carbines and machets being used frees
ly. Captain Baliat was the only gendaruG
wounded All the dead were colored Gu.
ban soldiers.


This morning payment was resumed under
heavy guard. There are rumors that a
force is being organized to attack the pay
office, but these are probably unfounded.


General Castillo, civil governor of Santa
go de Cuba, was at Cuevitas at the time and
soon restored order. There is no doubt that
the inaccurate list will cause great deal
of hardship. Many veterans have vainly
followed the United States commissioners
for six weeks, only to find that their names
are not listed. General Leonard Wood, mil
itary governor, does not, however, antici-
pate serious trouble.

MANILA, Nov. General Hughes,
commanding in the Visayan district, has
sent in an encouraging report. He says
the islanu of Negros is now more peaceful
and orderly than for twenty years. The
planters are pursuing their business un-
disturbed by the bands of brigands who
had long levied tribute on them. The
Americans have scattered the brigands
and propose to pursue them until they
are effectually suppressed.


General Young's column entered Caba-
nautuan, north of San Isidro, yesterday
morning. Colonel Parker, with two troops
of the Fourth Cavalry, took possession
of the deserted town of Aliaza.


Captain Batson captured telegraph
operator and his escort. finding tele-
gram to Aguinaldo from an insurgent
colonel reporting that General Lawton
was killed in a recent fight and that his
body had been sent to Manila. The oper-
ator said that 900 insurgents were ap-
preaching Aliaza from Tarlac. Batson
placed his scouts in ambush awaiting
them. Colonel Hayes, with four troops
of the Fourth Cavalry, charged the towns
of Talvarera and Cobal, dispensing $50
miles without any loss The Americans
captured two brass cannon and a guam
tity of ammunition, including many
Hotchkiss shells. Captain Batson took
storehOuse and ,ntities of rice, sugar,
corn and forty bull carts.


The steamer Lebuan of Hongkong, 500
tons, with a prize crew from the United
States gunboat Castine on board, has ar
rived here. She was captured while run
ming the blockade off Zamboanga She
had unloaded her cargo of merchandise.


All signs show that General Youngs
rapid advance is demoralizing the insur-
gents northward Prisoners report them
to be fleeing to the hills. There are many
deserters and sick men and the former
are taking their arms to the Americans.
The cayalry's rapid movements are
puzzle to the insurgents, who think that
the Americans in striking in so many
places must have overwhelming forces.


Aguinaldo is personally conducting the
campaign. He is asking the people for
rice and is trying to replenish the army
with recruits, but without success.

The editor of the War Cry is now a
benedict Last evening amid all the pomp
and splendor of hallelujah choruses
chanted by Salvation lads and lassies
and standing in bower of roses and
ferns Captain Alfred A Nickerson and
Captain Halle Sheffield were made hus-
band and wife.


Colonel William Evans pronounced the
solemn binding words, while Captain
Sawyer lent his support to the groom as
best man and Staff Captain Alice Bull at
tended the bride as maid of honor.


The wedding was celebrated at the
army headquarters at 1139 Market street,
and the vast hall was crowded with a
company that assisted in the merry
making that followed the ceremony The
bride wore no bridal finery. Her segula-
tion army garb did duty for the wedding
gown and the Salvation bonnet was worn
in lieu OF the regulation bridal VEIL The
only concession TO the happy occasion was
a wide white silk sash fastened over the
shoulder and falling in two long stream
ers from under the right arm. bunch
of fragrant white sweet peas formed the
brides bouquet and the maid carried a
bunch of pink carnations.


CAPTAIN and Mrs Nickerson will have
no honeymoon trip. They go Immediately
10 their cottage in Alameda and will con-
tinue without interruption their army
work there.

Her life when summed up and compared with the

good gift The blood within her little veins was

bership is anything like extensive her own She

1t is difficult to imagine a fortunate career

iii this mutable world. Love and power and wealth.
length OF years prosperity peace, honor children

in good health and with undsturbed heart she
celebrated her eghtieth birthday 1t is certainly
notable life which Victoria is rounding out into
old age and is strange that her people
scattered all over the globe rise up and call her

An expedition recently sent out from
England TO the Murray Islands has
brought some interesting information
about the islanders. These primitive peo-
pie. it appears, cannot count higher than
two. "Netat" is their word for one and
nets" for two. When they want to say
three they say "one-two" (netats-nets).
and when they want to say four they say
"two-two" (nets-nets).


Higher figures than these they express
by means of their bodies. Thus they be-
gan TO count from the little finger of the
left hand and proceeding thence to the
other fingers they successfully reach the
wrist the arm, the shoulder, the collar
bone, the chest. the right shoulder. the
right arm, the right wrist and finally the
fingers of the right hand. In this way
they can count as high as thirty-one.


When they want to express higher
number than this they can only use the
word ''gaire,' which signifies many. This
ancient method of counting, however, is
fast disappearing, thanks to the siren
uous efforts which the English are max
ing to teach the islanders the ordinary
rules of arithmetic. Ethnologists there
fore are especially glad that Information
about this ancient method of counting
has come to them just as II was on the
point of disappearing forever.

MANILA, August 10 (via Hong Kong.
August 22).-The Filipino rebels appear to
retain much more of a fighting spirit than
might be expected after their recent San
Fernando experiences ana General Law
ton drubbings in the south.


After giving up San Fernando with a
feeble struggle, they entreuched them
selves at Angeles. working for several
days and impressing non-combatants into
the work. thus saving the armed men for
the fighting. They engaged Lieutenant
Colonel Smiths regiment and the artillery
warmly for four hours. making one of the
most stubborn resistances of the campaign
But the Americans are indebted to the
usual poor workmanship Of the filipinos
as we'll as to their own strategy for their
small loss.


In the province of Cavite, where it was
supposed the rebels had been scattered and
dcmoralized beyond recuDeratiOn they
have assembled an army of several thou
sand men distributed among the important
tow ms from the lake to the bay.


After the San Fernando engagement the
rebels attempted to deter the Americans
from a further advance northward by
menaciHg the railroad communications.
Several hundred of General Pho del PilarS
Men crossed the Rio Grande, between the
American outpost towns, and threatened
EaHuag, Quingua and other places with
small American garrisons, while. during
Sunday and Monday nights, smaller bands
tried to tear up the railroad track at
eral points between Bigaa and Malolos.

ever, Were sent along The railroad from
Manila to Ssn Fernando. while the forces

Gen. Pho del Pillars men, and the rebels

In brushes between these Filipinos and
the Americans during three days the Amer
leans lost several men, while the Fflipinos'

American operations and to minimize the
olG'tsltlon- Gen. Otis says newspapers are

hundreds of people come into Manila

SEATTLE, April 26.-In broad daylight
early to-day the steamer Homer crashed
into the brigantine Blakeley, which was
moored fast to her dock, and almost cut
the vessel in halves amidships. This is
the second collision within two months
the Homer has had in daylight while
coming into her dock. In fact, the
steamer was on her way from the ship
yard where the injuries she sustained
when she collided with the Al-Ki had
just been repaired when she ran into the
Blakeley.


Captain Higgins of the Homer claims
the accident this morning was due to the
fact that the ropes to the bells in the
engine-room broke and he was unable to
control the steamer. The inspectors at
this point blamed the Homer for the AL
Ki collision, but on appeal to the Super
vising Inspectors at San Francisco this
decision was reversed and the Al-Ki then
brought suit for damages against the
Homer, which is pending. Captain Hig-
gins takes all the blame for the collision
to-day.


The Homer is again on the ways, and
the Blakeley, by shifting the cargo and
lifting the breach in her side above
water, is still at the dock.

Nothing In recent American history
has been more remarkable than the
stout and continued resistance Of the
New York stock and money markets to
the reaction which has long been con-
sidered inevitable from the great indus
trial and speculative boom OF last
spring. The rapid forming of trusts and
the placing Of their apparently profita-
bic stock upon the market In large
quantities seemed to be the last incl
dent necessary to revive confidence and
renew the monetary circulation after
the long depression Of the panic. The
pendulum swung widely toward
period Of imitation. There was for
time serious danger Of renewed collapse
and panic.


But three months have now passed
since the industrial speculation went to
its extreme limit. the New York stock
markets have gone through the dull
lapse Of summer. and there has yet TO
become manifest any sign Of serious
weakening. Railroad shares, as well
as industrials, have held their own
strongly against all adverse news and
influences. the money market has faced
out a marked tightness and general in
vestment activity has been resumed.


During May and June both Great
Britain and Germany were confronted
with serious financial conditions. and
heroic efforts were necessary to avert
evil consequences. Under ordinary cir
cumstances the American financiers
would have been responsive, and catas-
trophe. from apprehension. II from moth
ing else. would have fallen upon the
monetary centers of this country. But
the steady self-control Of the tremen-
dous interests which are directing the
capitalization Of American industrial or
ganizations seems to have exercised a
quieting effect elsewhere and to have
played favorably into the hands OF the
afflicted countries Of Europe. Within
the year past nearly SO per cent. OF the
American securities hitherto held
abroad have been repurchased by the
American investors. and the United
States Is thus made dependent upon no
conditions save those Of its own pros
perity.


still further factor making toward
financial stability has been the develop
ment of capitalistic and money-lend-
ing interest west OF the Atlantic coast.
During temporary construction in
money in New York in the latter part
of last month, Chicago. Minneapolis. st.
Paul. ST Louis. and even Denver and Sc
attic. offered loans In the metropolis and
relieved the situation when the banks
were overdrawn. The westward spread
ing Of capitalistic initiation has been de-
sirable for long time. It's present hap
pening virtually lifts the United States
from the possibility OF an uncontrolla-
BILE money panic. and guarantees a pros
perity that NAV continue so long as
the people abstain from overproduc-
ton and hold themselves within the
hounds Of rational enterprise and care
fal speculation.

An expedition recently sent out from Eng

cannot count higher than two. "Netat" is

When they want to say three they say

want to say four they say ''two-two'
(nets-nets).


Higher figures than these they express by
means of their bodies Thus they began TO
count from the little finger of the left hand
and proceeding thence to the other fingers
they successfully reach the wrist the arm
the shoulder, the collar bone, the chest the
right shoulder, the right arm, the right
wrist and finally the fingers of the right
hand. In this way they can count as high
as thfrty-one.


When they want to express a higher
number than this they can only use the
word "gaire," which signifies many This
ancient method of counting. however, is
fast disappearing. thanks to the strenu-
Gus efforts which the English are making
to teach the islanders the ordinary rules
OF arithmetic. Ethnologists therefore are
especially glad that information about this
ancient method of counting has come 10
them just as 1t was on the point of disap-
pearing forever.

The glorious Fourth is being celebrated

hundreds are spending the holiday at this
beautiful suburban resort. The electric
cars have been well filled ali day with hap
py youngsters and their parents, laden
with lunch baskets, fireworks and other
Fourth of July necessities, and thus far the
day has been a great success The picnic
grounds, with their fine old shade trees, ex-
cellent spring water, tables and benches

on the lake, the merry round, dancing
pavilion and other amusements have kept
the children busy when firecrackers lost
their charm. The swimming and tub races
started at pm. and will continue until 6
O'Clock, and perhaps longer. These aquatic
sports, together with the efforts of the boys
to climb the creased pole, have afforded
great amusement to all. Tonight there
will be grand display of fireworks and the
set pieces and the thousands of fairy lights
along the shore and on the lake will be
Illuminated. Prof. Joyce will also con-
tribute to the pleasure of the occasion by
his daring performance on the high wire
over the lake, and on the low dancing wire
Prof. Donch and his musicians furnish the
music for dancing in the big pavilion.

scarcely perceptible with the hulk hos ed

started for the open sea The tide car
ried the youngsters out some distance
before they were noticed. and a passing
tug had narrow escape from colliding

launch was secured and brought the cast

ened when they landed tnat they were
unable to tell their names. The Incl

water front, particularly when the big

tatives of the diplomatic corps, the army

thusiastic applause of the numbers, more
particularly the dance of all nations. in
which picturesquely attired and gracefully

ed Columbia and her sister nations


The applause following every feature of

neous and encores often could not be de-
MED.

The next best was the "hcwer Dance"

ure


Die Puppenfee" tells with pantomime,
music and dancing the story of German
toy shop, whose proprietor exhibits his
wares to arstocratic customers. Each prn
cipal doll and wax figure is taken from it's
pedestal by sturdy porter, played yes
terday by Prince Troubetskoy of amateur
athletic renown, and after being wound up
dances or sings as its make permits. Die
Puppenfee, or the fairy doll, finally is pur
chased by English noble folks, and then the
curtain falls on the first act. The next act
disCloses the shop and the toys at mid
night. A fairy queen appears, and with
wave of her wand gives life and gayety to
the dolls, and for time they enjoy them
selves in characteristic ways. At dawn the
shopkeeper. hearing noises, drowsily enters,
but fails to discover the cause and then,
with a final grouping of the figures, the
curtain descends for the last time.

Obadiah Barber, the veteran bear hunter
of the Okefinokee swamp, has told in his
day some hot bear stories, but now he
comes along with his latest yarn, which he
offers with implicit faith that the folk will
believe this also.


He says his neighbor, old man John Cra-
ven, who lives on Hickory Hammock an
island in the great Okefinokee swamp, has
tanned some alligators and given them to
his children as Il Dewey day present. Mr.
Craven caught the alligators several years
ago when they were in their swaddling
clothes, and built them a playhouse in his
back yard. The children We're soon on good
terms with them and taught them numer-
Gus useful and ridiculous tricks The ba-
Des were docile and in their sleepy-headed
way gradually awaited themselves of such
educational advantages the Craven chill
dren offered to them. But the alligators
are about grown now, measuring from eight
to nine feet each, and are exceedingly
athletic considering the clumsiness of their
fellow alligators in the swamp. And now
the children hitch the alligators to ploWs
and cultivate the potato patch with them.
Sometimes the boys ride the saurian over
the farm. An alligator wagon has been
made by the boys, and when they want to
take a straw ride they invite their sisters
and their neighbors' children over and all
take ride behind the two pet alligators.

STOCKTON. June 22.-The steamer
Captain Weber came in this morning with
a break in one of her boilers, through
which steam was escaping 1t extended
alongside line of rivets. The danger
was not known until the steamer was
quite near port, and every precaution was
at once taken to prevent serious conse-
quences. The passengers knew nothing
of the accident, as it was not deemed
necessary to create any alarm although
the consequences might have been terrible
but for the timely discovery and prompt
action. The Union Transportation Com
pany's officers took no chances and they
at once announced the boat would not
leave port tonight. The boiler-rooms
were turned over to machinists. The steel
around the crank was cut away and new
steel parts are being riveted in. The
Weber will be out in day or two and
before she resumes her runs the company
will have the machinery thoroughly in
spected. The boilers are comparatively
new and the break must have been the
result of a flaw. The Weber is one of the
best boats in the river service, and the
delay at this busy season involves con-
siderable loss to the company.

HONOLULU. Oct. s.-The transport
Centennial arrived from San Francisco on
the 5th She brought 300 horses. sixty of
them hanging in sings and ready to die
from simple exhaustion. Two Of them
died after reaching port, one breathing it's
last on the dock and the other in its sling
on the middle deck.


The horses had been at sea for eight
days. each one fastened to a stall Just
wide enough and long enough for its body
For eight days the suffering animals had
no sleep-no rest whatever. They stood
and kept balance with the rolling of the
ship. A few days more and many deaths
from exhaustion could not have been
avoided. The horses started as fresh
spirited animals. brought from Nevada
and Oregon. They arrived thin and jaded.
a large proportion of them only kept alive
by stimulants. About twenty gallons Of
alcohol were given to the horses during
the Centennials trip The animals were
unloaded here and will be turned out to
pasture until the return of the transport
from San Francisco.

RED. BLUFF, Aug. 13.-Telephone re-
ports from Lyonsville give news of the
destruction of the lumber yard there this
morning The fire started near the rear
end Of the Champion mill, and the entire
yard was destroyed. The mill and build
ings were saved. The property belongs
to the Sierra Lumber Company, of which
Peter Dean of San Francisco is president.
Superintendent Ransom was absent from
town. There were two or three million
feet of lumber in the yard. The sash, door
and box factory of Red Bluff was largely
supplied from the Champion mill The fire
will probably cripple local operations.

ley and the extreme Southern California.

One Of the most thoroughly enjoyable

LONDON. Dec. 6.-The Daily Telegraph

correspondent:


MODDER RIVER, Thursday afternoon.
Nov. SO.-Lord Methuen's troops are al
rest here for few days after their ire
mendous eXertions recently. During the
night on Tuesday the enemys fire was
simply terrific throughout the day. Two
OF our batteries-the Eighteenth and the
Seventy-hfth-bore the brunt Of the battle
and discharged no fewer than 1000 rounds
the Seventy-ffth shelling the town all day
at range Of 200 yards and at last having
10 retire for want of ammunition Just
before they withdrew a tremendous fire
was concentrated on them by the Beers.
Major Lindsay and Captain Ferrall were
wounded and two men were killed and
eleven wounded.


Twenty-Five horses were lost and OFF,
GERS chargers had TO be used TO bring the
battery back. Major Lindsay and Captain
Ferrall had to walk out of action One
gallant driver. though shot through the
lung. drove his gun out. The Maxim de-
tachment Of the Scots Guard. under Lieu
tenant Elweys, was completely wiped out
when they advanced TO attack the en-
emys trenches. So we'll hidden were the
Beers that our men, though under their
fire, could not see them. Lieutenant
Thorpe crossed the river on the left flank
with a company OF Argyle and Sutherland
Highlanders and held his position until
the brigade could cross. The Highlanders'
loss was very severe. They had TO move
across TO support our left. and as soon as
they showed themselves they were moved
down. Regardless of the fusillade, how
ever. they went across in d quiet and
leisurely manner.


Captain George Nugent cantered about
with orders on a white pony, drawing a
tremendous fire from the enemy but he
miraculously escaped unhurt Lord
Methuens original intention was to take
the town with the bayonet after dark, but
his troops were too exhausted after their
tremendously hard day. They had started
without any breakfast and obtained no
food or water until o'clock at night. The
enemy got his guns away. but left many
rifles and quantities of ammunition be-
hind.


We communicated with Kimberley by
means of a searchlight last night The
bridge over the Modder was destroyed by
putting up their own. The railway was
also damaged. but the engineers repaired
IL in wonderfully quick time.


Lord Methuen is doing well. The Beers
occupy a strong ridge six miles TO the
north. The Lancers were in contact with
them to-day.

The September hot wave has come some
what early in the month, and 1t may there
fore not prove to be the only visitation Of
caloric which this section of the country
will have before fall weather actually sets
in. Yesterday the western cities suffered
from unprecedented temperatures, the
weather bureau records being broken in
many places. Fortunately, however, a
high developed soon afterward, bringing
in cooler airs from the north and thus end
ing the heated spell in short order. The
rising temperatures in Washington today
indicate that the heat wave has travelled
faster than usual Today's record shows
an almost uniform rise of fourteen degrees
ever yesterday, bringing the temperature
into the midsummer range. If the cool
airs which have already brought relief to
the west shall continue to flow eastward
the local sufferings may not be prolonged,

Have you ever tried brushing your hair
the wrong way? I know a little woman
whose hair had long been thin and -scraggy.
She was in despair, having used a host of
different tonics without benefit, when a
French maid suggested brushing the hair
the wrong way, assuring her mistress that
In Paris this was favorite way of groom
ing the hair.


The American woman decided to try the
experiment. Her maid carefully divided the
hair into many small parts, and then, with
a huge and very stiff brush, began her
work. Holding the extreme end of the
strand to be brushed in her left hand, she
started at the bottom of 1t and brushed up
ward toward the head. After each strand
mad gone through this process the maid
snoothed each hair back into it's original
position.


Now the woman brushes her hair in this
manner each night and morning. She de-
ciares 1t has proved more beneficial than an
expensive tonic.

BUFFALO, n. Y, Jan. blocked
IN a huge ice foe, the Canadian ferry
Niagara, with nineteen persons on
board was swept hopelessly down the
Niagara River tonight and dismantled
by the international bridge. The boat.
which plies between this city and Erie,
Ont, left her dock near the mouth of
the river in the early evening on her
last trip of the day, having on board
fifteen passengers, six of whom were
women and two children. Her crew
consisted of four men. The river was
full Of floating ice that was drifting in
from Lake Erie, but the boat, heading
diagonally against the current, made
her way to the center of the stream,
Here she became imbedded in a great
field of ice and her engines were power
less to propel her. The current at this
point is exceedingly swift and the mo-
mentum of the ice field carried the
ferry with it,


The passengers, realizing their situa-
ton, were horror stricken with the fear
of being carried over the falls, and the
more imminent danger of being dashed
against a pier of the international
bridge. The calls of the ferry whistle
attracted attention from the shore, and
fire tugs were started out a mile above
to rescue the helpless craft.


The passengers and crew of the
Niagara put on life-preservers and
stood with blanched faces while the
boat swept onward. River navigation
being closed, the draws of the bridge
are imperative and the draw engines
dead. 1t was evident that the upper
works of the boat could not clear the
span, but the great menace was the
piers of solid masonry.


The current favored the boat and
swept her between the span, a little to
the east side of the ce1-ter of the river
The iron Orders of the bridge raked
the boat clean of her second deck. car
rying away smokestack, pilothouse and
hurricane deck. The passengers and
crew were below deck and escaped in
jury from the wreckage. Swinging
clear of the bridge the Niagara broke
free from the foe and drifted into a
path of clear water. A sand gear was
attached to the rudder. the engines,
which were uninjured resumed their
duty and the dismembered craft was
slowly worked to the dock on the
American shore.

LAYGAN ALBERTO, June 3.-Between
twenty-five and thirty Indians, including
men, women and children, were drowned
yesterday in Lake of the Clouds, near ne
Canadian Pacific Railway, while crossing
the reservation to attend potlatch. They
were travelling in boats, rudely manufac-
tured of the skins of cariboo and other
animals, when two long boats collided.
Both vessels were rendered useless, and
the entire party was lost.


The third vessel bearing the skins of
deer, bear, cariboo, mountain sheep and
goats, and manned by four Indians,
reached the spot as the last survivor
slipped from the capsized boat and dis
appeared in the glacier-fed waters of
the lake. A dense cloud resting on the
surface of the lake was responsible for
the accident.

text:
Three years after the memorable frost
that killed three-fourths OF her orange trees
down to the roots n cold wave has again
invaded Florida, herorange industry is once
more FRUSTRATED, and the damage cannot be
repaired for several years.


Last season was a poor orange year, but
fruit from the trees that sprang from the
old roots was coming into the market and
the crop was about half as great as that
yielded the year before the disaster. About
forty per cent. OF the orange growers, dis
heartened by their former misfortune. had
abandoned the business. Those who hope
fully kept on find all hopes of profit blasted
again for years to come. In the large orange
district of Deland, about 100 miles south Of
Jacksonville, all the trees have been killed,
n in the more southern districts the
groves are said to have been badly hurt.


Orange growers said last year that the
Florida crop would not reach its former
proportions for ten years, and many be-
lieved that the crop would never again
reach its old magnitude. The result of
this new misfortune will he to increase
the present tendency in Florida to sub
stitute other crops for oranges Many
orange growers have already turned their
attention to other products and have pros
pered. They are growing tobacco and hay,
and not a few have gone into stock raising.
More attention is now given to pine
apples, and though the pineries were dam
aged by this cold wave, the loss will not be
very great, for the plant is grown partly
under cover to protect it from the fierce
Florida sun.


OF course there will now he a fresh boom
in California orange culture. The present
tariff on all citrus fruits has practically
stopped orange importations, but even if
Florida goes out Of the business we may
still grow all the oranges We can consume.
California's crop last year, about 5000, 900
boxes, was larger than the worlds output
not many years ago.

text:
FRESNO, Sept 3.-Mrs. Anna Wills
and her infant son Alex lost their lives
in a fire which occurred at Sanger, in
this county, last night. The mother
was seriously injured while trying to
rescue her child and died shortly after
the fire. The infant was burned to
crisp and the charred body was not
found until 10 o'clock this morning.


Mrs. Wills was at home alone with
her child last evening. She went out
side for a few minutes. leaving the in
fant sleeping in its cradle and a coal
oil lamp burning in the front room. She
had not been outside very long when
her attention was attracted by a loud
report and looking around saw her
house in flames. The lamp which had
been left burning in the front room had
exploded, scattering blazing oil in all
directions.


The mothers first thought was to
rescue her child. She rushed back into
the burning building and through the
flames toward the room where she had
left the infant sleeping. One step
through the fire, however, and her
senses forsook her. She reeled, stag
gered and fell backward through the
door she had just entered. Her cloth
ing was on fire and her face and hands
were already badly burned. Neighbors
who had been attracted by the fire
came to her assistance and rescued her,
but not until the clothing had been
burned from her body. She was un-
conscious, but revived long enough to
tell the story of the disaster and then
expired Iamenting the fate Of her child.


AS soon as the building had been re-
duced to ashes a search was begun for
the remains of the infant. So COM
pletely had the child been burned. how
ever. that no trace Of the body was dis
covered for nearly twelve hours.


AS soon after the catastrophe as pos
sible an effort was made to communi-
cate the facts TO Coroner Long in this
city. but the telephone lines were down
and the news of the accident did not
reach Fresno until o'clock this morn
ing. Coroner Long then went to
Sanger to hold the inquest over the re-
mains of mother and child.


The dead woman was one of the
best-known residents of Sanger and
had a wide circle of friends. AS nearly
az could be learned the explosion was
caused by a gust of wind entering
through the front door. When Mrs.
wills went out she closed the door, but
IT is thought the latch did not work
and that the wind blew 1t open.

CHICAGO, December 20.-A special to the
Record from San Francisco says:
After a most tempestuous voyage across
the Pacific, the United States transport
Sikh arrived here today, three DAYS over
due. The trip from Manila was one of the
stormiest yet encountered by the Sikh, and
she came into port badly battered by the
waves and wind. On December 6 the boat
was struck by a storm that continued to
rage for many days The gale tore the fun
mel loose. broke the cables that support the
aftermast, and the foremast was half torn
from its stays. AS last resort the Sikh
was headed into the wind for safety


For forty-four hours the ship lay help
less, with engines going at half speed, with
out gaining mile. At last the funnel was
made fast during the gale, being secured
by guy ropes. The masts were made fast
in the same manner, and the vessel made
Its way to port.


The Attack on Cavite.


By the transport Rio Janeiro were receiv-
ed the first details of the recent Filipino at
tack on the Cavite navy yard. The insur-
gents planned an attack on Fort Rice and
under cover of this. which they thought
would draw all the American troops to that
point, they proposed to steal over from
Cavite Viejo in feet of boats and capture
the navy yard and arsenal. Everything
proceeded as planned and the rebels In
small boats were only a little way from
shore, when they encountered danger from
an unexpected quarter


The searchlight of the gunboat Petrol
beamed upon them. Then well-aimed shots
from the Petrol caused the rebels to turn
about in hot haste and paddle desperately to
reach shore. One siX-pound shell from the
Petrol struck an insurgent boat amidships
knocked 1t to splinters and killed every
rebel on board. The others were beached
bear the mouth of a creek, and the Fill
pnos scattered inland.


Soldiers Bring Much Loot.


From trustworthy sources it was learned
that the two companies of Montana volun-
teers. who came back from Manila on the
transport Zealandia, brought back with
them S150000 in gold and Mexican silver.
This treasure was first discovered by two
men at Caloocan. They were the first to
enter the Filipino town, which was very
rich. They entered a mansion, but found
the place deserted In the garden they
saw traces of earth having been recently
disturbed Digging down they discovered
chest, which contained thousands of dol
lars in gold coin. The men who found the
gold treasure took all they could carry.
Then they uncovered q large chest full Of
Mexican dollars.


The Grant to Sail Today.


SAN FRANCISCO, Cal, December 20
The transport Grant will sail for Manila
this afternoon with the 4Sth Infantry (col-
ored). The postal authoritines put aboard
of her last night three wagonloads of mail
for Honolulu and the Philippines.


The transport Sikh, which arrived In bal
last, is to be released from the government
service.

SAN DOMINGO, Sept. 4.--A crisis was
reached in the monetary situation to-day.
Merchants refused to take paper money
and the people were unable to purchase
food. This resulted In serious disturb
ances in the market place this morning
and great disorder prevailed.


A Cabinet meeting was hurriedly called
and a proclamation practically demon
etizing paper money, except In part pay
ment of customs duties, was issued. The
proclamation was Kissed and is certain
to cause great dissatisfaction and suf-
fering.


General Caceres has resigned as Minis
ter of War and Aristides Patins, former
Minister, succeeds him. The Government
promises relief when Congress meets, but
the people demand immediate action.
