THE MARCHIONESS OF SALISBURY.


London. Nov 20-Lady Salisbury. wife Of the
Premier died this afternoon at Hatfield House.
Her health recently appeared to be improving
and her death to-day was unexpected


Georeiana Caroline Marchioness Of Salisbury
was the daughter of Sir George Hall Alderson
Baron OF the Exchequer. and the niece of Mrs
Opie. the novelist She married to Lord
Salisbury (who was then Lord Robert CeciD on
July IL. 1857. Her husband was then twenty
seven years Old while she some years his
senior.


Four years before. her husband had been
elected Fellow OF All Souls College. oxford.
and had been returned TO Parliament for STAN
ford. The early years of their married life were
passed in comparative obscurity. They had lit
tie money and lived in lodgings off the Strand.
The future Prime Minister added to his slender
income by writing. This he did for The
Times The Morning Chronicle" and The
Saturday Review" and the quarterlies. In 1868
Lord Robert Cecil became Viscount Cranborne,
and heir to the Marquisate through the death
OF his eldest brother. 1t was then that his
political career really began. AS her husband
advanced in rank and station Lady Salisbury
filled every place with grace and tact With
advancing years she grew to care less for social
functions but until her Illness some years
ago, she never remiss in her duties as
hostess, and when her husband has been in
office these have been Of the most onerous char
acter


Lord and Lady Salisbury have had five sons
and three daughters. one of the latter died in
1861 The Niscount Cranborne. born
in 1861: the Rev. Lord Rupert William Ernest
Cecil. Lord Edgar Algernon Robert Cecil,
barrster at law; Lieutenant Lord Edward Her
bert Cecil OF the Grenadier Guards. and Lord
Hugh Richard Heathcote Cecil. NJ p. The sur
vivng daughters are Lady Gwendolen Cecil and
the Countess Of SelbOrne. who was formerly
Lady Beatrix Maude Cecil.


Lady Salisbury had been in poor health for
many years, and in July suffered a second stroke
of paralysis. Since then her health had been
precarious. Lord Salisbury has been constant
in his devotion to her and in order 10 be with
her has for many months turned over as much
Of the public business as possible 10 other
hands. There have for some time been per
sistent rumors that in the event Of the death or
his wife Lord Salisbury would as soon as pos
sible retire from public life.

The moccasin is the most rational and
comfortable of all footwear. In moccasns
the feet have full play; they can bend and
grasp; there IS nothing to chafe them or
impede circulation. In moccasins one can
move like an acrobat, crossing slender and
slippery logs, climbing trees or passing
with ease and security along dizzy trails
on the mountainside where a slip might
mean sure destruction. The feet do not
stick fast N mud In the north, when the
mercury is far below zero and no civilized
boot will protect the feet from freezing,
the savage suffers no Inconvenience. HIS
moccasins, stuffed with dried gras let the
blood course freely. The persplration may
freeze on the hay in solid lump of ice, but
the feet remain warm end dry. The buck
skin moccasin. Indian-tanned with deers'
brains and wood smoke, always dries soft
after wetting.


in autumn, when all the leaves and twigs
are dry as finder, a man wearing shoes
makes noise in the forest like a troop of
cavalry, but in mOccasins he can move
swiftly through the woods with the stealth
of panther. The feet are not bruised for,
after enjoying for q time the freedom of nat
ural covering, these hitherto laundering
members become like hands, and feel their
way through the dark like those of a cat
avoiding obstacles as though gifted with
special sense. Best of all, the moccaSin is
light inexperienced sportsmen and SOL
diers affect high-topped lace boots with
heavy soles and hObnails imagining that
these are the most serViceabie for rough
wear. But these boots weigh between four
and five pounds. while d pair of thick
moosc-hide moccasins weigh only eleven
ounces. In marching ten miles a man
wearing the clumsy boots lifts twenty tons
more shoe leather than if he wore mecca
sins.

SACRAMENTO, April 16.-The heroic
spectacle of a woman so years old sur
rendering her life in the hope of pro-
tecting the life of her infant grand
daughter was presented in this city
this evening Mrs. Christian Miller of
300S F street had gone to the evening
service at church, leaving her one-year-
old daughter in the care of Mrs. Cath
crime Woods, the grandmother, so years
of age. The child was seated in a
high chair near the table, upon which
burned reading lamp. The aged
woman engaged herself in reading
while the child prattled away.


The little one was playful, and, seiz-
ing the tablecloth, gave it jerk. The
force was not great but 1t was suffi-
cient to dislodge the lamp. The next
instant the clothes Of the baby were
ablaze. Terrified, and yet with some
presence of mind the S0-year-old grand
mother righted the lamp and seized the
child in her arms. Out of the house she
ran with the screaming infant, pressing
it to her bosom in an effort to smother
the flames that were consuming its
clothes and scorching its tender flesh.


Once in the garden Mrs. Woods rolled
the child in the grass, hoping to put
out the fire, and succeeding measur-
ably. Meantime the flames were en-
comprising the little home; and mean
while also the fire which had caught
from the child's clothing was bent upon
the destruction of her own life. Neigh
bors saw the old woman, her clothing
af1ame, run toward the burning house.
Ten minutes afterward her blackened
body was found just outside the door
way. Every vestige of clothing had
been burned away. When Mrs. Miller
returned from church she found her
home sadly damaged by fire, her mother
dead and her child frightfully burned,
though still alive.
